# The Space Between Thoughts

I'm sitting in a coffee shop at 3 PM on a Tuesday, and I've just realized I don't know what time it is where you are. This thought arrived unbidden, like most of the ones I'm about to share. Time zones seem like one of humanity's more creative solutions to an awkward problem—not quite lies, but definitely workarounds.

There's a woman across from me typing furiously on her laptop. Every thirty seconds, she stops, stares at the wall, and then returns to typing. I wonder if she's fighting with words or if the words are fighting with her. Maybe they're dancing. I prefer to think it's dancing.

Someone once told me that the secret to happiness is lowered expectations, but I think they were just having a bad day. The real secret is probably something embarrassingly simple that we all know but keep forgetting, like "drink water" or "call your mother." I'm not going to tell you what I think it is because I'm not confident enough, and also, I keep forgetting it myself.

I ordered a cappuccino and they brought me a latte. I could say something, but I won't. It tastes fine. This feels like a metaphor for something—accepting what you didn't ask for—but I don't want to push it. Not every moment needs to mean something. Sometimes a wrong coffee is just a wrong coffee, and the beautiful part is that it's still drinkable.

There's an art to complaining versus an art to letting things go, and I think people spend their whole lives never quite learning either one properly. They just rotate between them like a malfunctioning dial. Complain too much and you become exhausting; complain too little and you become a ghost haunting your own life, present but not accounted for.

I've been thinking about how we're all just making it up as we go, which is either the most liberating thought or the most terrifying one, depending on what time of day it is. Right now it feels liberating. Ask me again at 11 PM and I might tell you something different.

The woman with the laptop just closed it suddenly. She seems relieved. I wonder if she finished what she was working on or if she just surrendered to it. Both feel like valid endings.

I think about how every person in this coffee shop has an entire universe inside their head—complete with its own logic, memories, fears, inside jokes with themselves. The barista is making someone's drink with the same hands he's been using all day, and nobody thinks about how his hands contain someone's entire universe. We're walking around carrying infinite universes in our skulls, bumping into each other, mostly trying not to think about it.

Someone's phone buzzes. Someone else's buzzes back. It's like watching birds communicate, except more anxious and addictive.

I've never understood why we're so afraid of silence. Silence gets a bad reputation. People fill it with small talk and music and podcasts, but silence is just the space between heartbeats, and we're doing fine in that space most of the time. Our hearts don't panic during silence. They just keep going.

There's something beautiful about being a beginner at everything. Children seem to understand this. They're always trying things, failing, and trying again without the narrative we adults construct—the one where failure is permanent and means something definitive about your worth. Kids just think it means you try differently next time. What happened to that?

I think I lost it somewhere around the age where people started asking me what I wanted to be when I grew up. As if growing up meant crystallizing into one specific shape, forever. As if you get to choose at age seven who you'll be for the next sixty years.

The cappuccino—or latte, I guess—is getting cold. I'm not going to drink it. I'm just going to leave it here and watch what happens to it. Nothing, probably. Evaporation. The slow return to the universe of one less warm beverage.

I've been wondering lately if meaning is something we find or something we create. This feels like it should have a definitive answer, but I suspect the real answer is "yes," which is unsatisfying in the way that honest answers often are.

Someone just walked in looking like they're having the worst day of their life. I wonder if it actually is, or if it just feels that way because they haven't had enough water. Or sleep. Or both. I want to tell them that things get better, but I don't know their situation. Maybe things won't get better. Maybe things will just change, which is different. Usually better, sometimes worse, but always different. At least there's that.

The light coming through the window is doing that thing where it makes dust particles visible. All this light, always traveling, always arriving, always trying to show us things. We mostly ignore it because it's constant. We only notice light when there's darkness to compare it to. This seems like a metaphor too, but again, I'm not going to push it.

I'm going to get up soon. I'm going to leave money on the table—a little extra for the cappuccino-latte confusion. I'm going to step out into the Tuesday afternoon, where it's probably still 3 PM somewhere and also definitely not 3 PM somewhere else. The world will keep spinning through its zones and its times and its different versions of "now."

And I'll probably forget most of what I was thinking about here, which is fine. These weren't meant to be permanent. They were just the space between thoughts—the ones I'm catching on the way to the ones I'll actually hold onto.

That's probably more honest than I usually am.
